title: Looping with <= over an array
question:
prices = [10, 20, 30], indexes start at 0, and the language checks every array access. What happens when this runs?

sum ← 0
i ← 0
while i <= length(prices)
    sum ← sum + prices[i]
    i ← i + 1
options: sum ends at 60 and the loop exits normally
sum ends at 50, because the first price is skipped
The loop runs forever, because <= never becomes false
An index-out-of-range error is raised when i is 3
explanation: A 3-element array has the valid indexes 0, 1 and 2. With i <= length(prices) the loop also runs for i = 3, and reading prices[3] raises an out-of-range error after sum has already reached 60. The fix is i < length(prices), or a for-each loop that needs no index at all. Every access is checked, so no element is skipped and the loop does not run forever; without bounds checks the read would silently access memory past the array instead.

title: break inside a nested loop
question:
What does this code print?

for i from 0 to 2
    for j from 0 to 2
        if j = 1 then break
        print(i, j)
options: 0 0, then 1 0, then 2 0 (one pair per line)
Only 0 0, because break leaves both loops
Nothing, because break runs before any print
explanation: break ends only the innermost loop that contains it. For each i, the inner loop prints i 0, reaches j = 1 and breaks, and the outer loop then moves on to the next i, so the output is 0 0, 1 0 and 2 0. Skipping j = 1 and carrying on would need continue, and leaving both loops at once needs a flag, a labelled break where the language has one, or a return from a function.

title: Finding the largest value, starting from 0
question:
A helper returns the largest number in a non-empty list:

function largest(nums)
    best = 0
    for i from 0 to length(nums) - 1
        if nums[i] > best then best = nums[i]
    return best

What does largest([-8, -3, -5]) return, and what is the fix?
options: 0; start best at nums[0] instead of 0
-3; the function already handles negatives
-8; compare with >= best instead of > best
-5; the loop keeps the last value it sees
explanation: No element is greater than the starting value 0, so best is never updated and the function returns 0, a number that is not even in the list. Starting from the first element (best = nums[0]) makes the answer come from the data. Changing > to >= does not help, since no negative number is >= 0. Test edge cases such as all-negative values, a single element and an empty list.

title: Two loops, one after the other
question:
users has n items and orders has m items. What is the tightest Big O for this function, assuming each print takes constant time?

function report(users, orders)
    for i from 0 to length(users) - 1
        print(users[i].name)
    for j from 0 to length(orders) - 1
        print(orders[j].total)
options: O(n × m), one step per user-order pair
O(n + m), one pass over each list
O(n²), since there are two loops
O(log(n + m)), since print is cheap
explanation: The loops run one after the other, not nested: the first does n constant-time steps and the second does m, so the total is n + m steps, which is O(n + m). Multiplying to n × m is only right when one loop runs inside the other. O(n²) both ignores m and assumes nesting, and nothing here halves the input, so there is no logarithm.

title: Mixing AND and OR without parentheses
question:
A checkout grants a discount with:

discount = isMember OR total > 100 AND NOT isBanned

A banned member (isMember = true, isBanned = true) with total = 50 still gets the discount. Under the precedence rules used by almost every language, why?
options: OR binds tighter: (isMember OR total > 100) AND NOT isBanned
Mixed AND and OR are always grouped strictly from left to right
> binds loosest, so it reads (isMember OR total) > (100 AND NOT isBanned)
AND binds tighter: isMember OR (total > 100 AND NOT isBanned)
explanation: In boolean algebra and in virtually every mainstream language, AND has higher precedence than OR, much as multiplication binds tighter than addition, so the expression means isMember OR (total > 100 AND NOT isBanned). Since isMember is true, the whole OR is true and the ban never matters. The intended rule needs parentheses: (isMember OR total > 100) AND NOT isBanned. Grouping left to right, or with OR binding tighter, would give exactly that intended (false) result, and comparison operators such as > bind tighter than both AND and OR.

title: Combining bit flags with |
question:
A permission system uses bit flags:

READ = 1    (binary 001)
WRITE = 2   (binary 010)
EXEC = 4    (binary 100)

perms = READ | EXEC

What is perms, and is WRITE set?
options: true, since | is a logical OR of two non-zero values
5, and perms & WRITE is 2, so WRITE is set
5, and perms & WRITE is 0, so WRITE is not set
4, since | keeps only the higher of the two flags
explanation: | is bitwise OR: 001 | 100 sets both bits and gives 101, which is 5. A flag is tested with bitwise AND: 101 & 010 is 0, so WRITE is not set. A logical OR works on whole truth values instead of combining bits, and | never drops a bit that is set in either operand.

title: Two variables, one object
question:
Account is a class, and object variables hold references to objects, as in most object-oriented languages:

a = new Account(balance: 100)
b = a
b.balance = 50
b = new Account(balance: 10)
print(a.balance)

What is printed?
options: 50: b changed the shared object, then pointed elsewhere
100: b = a copied the object, so a never changed
10: a and b stay linked, so a follows b to the new object
0: the first object is collected once b moves away
explanation: An object variable holds a reference, so b = a copies the reference and both variables point to the same object; b.balance = 50 is therefore visible through a. Assigning a new object to b only changes where b points; it does not touch a or the object a refers to. That object is still reachable through a, so it cannot be reclaimed. Only a value type, copied on assignment, would make b an independent copy.

title: A recursive search that returns nothing
question:
This recursive binary search over a sorted array (indexes start at 0) should return 3 for find([1, 3, 5, 7, 9], 7, 0, 4), but the caller gets no value back:

function find(a, target, lo, hi)
    if lo > hi then return -1
    mid = floor((lo + hi) / 2)
    if a[mid] == target then return mid
    if a[mid] < target then
        find(a, target, mid + 1, hi)
    else
        find(a, target, lo, mid - 1)

What is the bug?
options: mid is computed wrongly, so index 3 is never examined
The recursive results are discarded; both calls need return
The base case fires too early, so its -1 is lost on the way
The else branch should search lo to mid, not lo to mid - 1
explanation: The first call sees a[2] = 5 < 7 and recurses; the inner call finds 7 at index 3 and returns 3, but the outer call ignores that value and reaches the end of the function without returning anything. Every recursive branch must pass its result back up: return find(a, target, mid + 1, hi), and the same for the else branch. Index 3 is examined, the base case is never reached here, and searching lo to mid - 1 is right because a[mid] has already been checked.
